new.title: Stand under Charlemagne's octagon
new.desc: Charlemagne had this chapel built around 800 and is still buried here, in a gold and silver shrine. For six centuries German kings were crowned here and then took their seat on his plain stone throne in the west gallery.
new.tip: On the way in, feel inside the lion's mouth on the bronze Wolfstür: legend says the devil lost his thumb there after the townspeople tricked him.

new.title: Meet Charlemagne's golden bust in the Domschatzkammer
new.desc: The cathedral treasury is one of the richest church treasuries north of the Alps, with the Gothic bust of Charlemagne, the Lothar Cross and his hunting knife.
new.tip: Combine it with a guided cathedral tour from the Dom-Information in the same building: the tour is the easy way to get close to the throne.

new.title: Walk into the Coronation Hall of the Rathaus
new.desc: Aachen's Gothic town hall was built on the walls of Charlemagne's palace, and its upstairs hall hosted the coronation banquets of the Holy Roman kings. Today the Charlemagne Prize is awarded here.
new.tip: Young people living in the Städteregion get in free, so bring a student or local friend along.

new.title: Get the story straight at Centre Charlemagne
new.desc: The city museum on the Katschhof, between cathedral and town hall, walks you from Roman spa town to Charlemagne's capital and modern border city.
new.tip: Step out onto the Katschhof afterwards: it was the courtyard of Charlemagne's palace, with the Dom on one side and the Rathaus on the other.

new.title: Brave the sulphur smell at the Elisenbrunnen
new.desc: This neoclassical colonnade from 1827 pipes up warm thermal water from Aachen's springs, the reason the Romans and Charlemagne came here in the first place. You will smell it before you see it.
new.tip: Put a finger in the stream rather than drinking a glass: the water is officially classed as a medicine. The Tourist Info is in the same building.

new.title: Move the dolls of the Puppenbrunnen
new.desc: Bonifatius Stirnberg's bronze fountain from 1975 is made for touching: the jointed figures of a bishop, a professor, a market woman, a jester and a rider stand for Aachen life, and you can bend their arms and heads.
new.tip: Pose the figures for a photo of your own, then walk around the corner to the cathedral; it is a good stop with kids.

new.title: Watch out for the Bahkauv on the Büchel
new.desc: The Bahkauv is Aachen's own monster, a creature said to jump on the backs of drunk men coming home at night and make them carry it. Its bronze statue guards a small fountain on the Büchel.
new.tip: The Büchel is also where the old pubs are, so the legend is a fitting warning before a night out.

new.title: Catch the Hühnerdieb in the act
new.desc: On the Hühnermarkt a bronze thief runs off with his loot, only to discover he grabbed a crowing rooster that will give him away. A favourite of local children since 1913.
new.tip: Make it a fountain hunt: the Fischpüddelchen on the Fischmarkt and the Karlsbrunnen on the Markt are a few minutes away.

new.title: Follow the money at the Geldbrunnen
new.desc: The fountain 'Kreislauf des Geldes' shows how money circulates, with bronze figures of greed, stinginess, patronage and begging around a spiralling basin. The water runs year round, kept from freezing by the thermal springs.
new.tip: Look at the faces up close: the misers clutching their coins are the funniest part.

new.title: Find the Roman columns on the Hof
new.desc: This small triangular square sits on top of a Roman bath and temple complex, recalled today by a reconstructed portico of columns. It feels like a hidden courtyard a minute from the cathedral.
new.tip: It is the quiet place to sit with a coffee; at night the Domkeller next door takes over.

new.title: Pass through the Ponttor
new.desc: One of only two medieval city gates still standing, the 14th century Ponttor closes off the student street Pontstraße at its northern end.
new.tip: Walk the whole Pontstraße from the Markt to the gate and you have seen Aachen's student life in ten minutes.

new.title: Take a village break in Kornelimünster
new.desc: This old abbey village on the Inde, where a Benedictine abbey was founded in 814, still belongs to Aachen. The former abbey buildings now hold modern art, and the church keeps relics of Christ and of Pope Cornelius.
new.tip: Take the bus from the centre, or come by bike along the Vennbahn path, which passes right by the village.

new.title: Watch the sunset from the Lousberg
new.desc: The hill north of the old town is the city's favourite viewpoint, with the cathedral and the RWTH towers at your feet. Legend says it is a pile of sand the devil dropped after a market woman outwitted him.
new.tip: Look out for the hammocks near the top and grab one early on warm evenings.

new.title: Soak in hot spring water at the Carolus Thermen
new.desc: Aachen is officially 'Bad Aachen', and this spa on the edge of the Stadtgarten lets you swim in the same thermal water the Romans used, indoors and outdoors.
new.tip: Ideal on a rainy day; the sauna area is a separate, larger world if you have the whole afternoon.

new.title: Look for the hot springs of Burtscheid
new.desc: Burtscheid's springs are even hotter than those in the centre, up to about 74 degrees. Spa guests once boiled eggs in the Kochbrunnen, and the Kurpark from the late 18th century is the oldest park in Aachen.
new.tip: Start at the thermal fountain on the Burtscheider Markt, then walk into the Kurpark behind it; on Friday mornings there is a market.

new.title: See Warhol in an umbrella factory at the Ludwig Forum
new.desc: The Ludwig Forum shows the modern art collection of the chocolate couple Peter and Irene Ludwig, with Pop Art by Warhol, Lichtenstein and Haring, in a former umbrella factory.
new.tip: It is a short walk from the Ponttor out along Jülicher Straße; check the programme for its late evening openings.
new.q: Ludwig Forum für Internationale Kunst, Jülicher Straße 97, Aachen

new.title: Cycle the Vennbahn over the Kornelimünster viaducts
new.desc: The old railway from Aachen into the Venn is now a gentle cycle path. Inside the city it crosses two stone viaducts over 20 metres high, the Rollefbach and Iterbach viaducts.
new.tip: Have a drink in the old Kornelimünster station, now a restaurant, and keep riding south if you want to continue towards Monschau and Belgium.

new.title: Drink Glühwein between Dom and Rathaus
new.desc: Aachen's Christmas market fills the squares around the cathedral and town hall and ranks among the most beautiful in Germany, with Printen stalls everywhere.
new.tip: Come on a weekday evening: the weekends draw coach tours from across the Netherlands and Belgium.

new.title: Join the horse crowd at the CHIO in the Soers
new.desc: Every summer the Soers hosts the CHIO, billed as the world's biggest equestrian festival, with show jumping, dressage, eventing, driving and vaulting.
new.tip: You do not need a stadium ticket to soak up the atmosphere: a day ticket gets you onto the grounds with the side arenas and stalls.

new.title: Ride the rides at the Öcher Bend
new.desc: Aachen's big funfair goes back to at least 1413 and comes twice a year to the Bendplatz, at Easter and in summer. It always ends with fireworks on the last evening.
new.tip: Locals say 'dann ess evver der Bend op' when someone is about to get into trouble; drop it into conversation for a laugh.

new.title: Shout 'Oche Alaaf' at the Rose Monday parade
new.desc: Carnival is serious business in Aachen, and the Rosenmontagszug of the AKV, founded in 1859, brings over a hundred floats and marching groups through the centre, ending with the Carnival Prince.
new.tip: Bring a bag for the Kamelle (sweets) thrown from the floats and dress up; you will stand out more without a costume.

new.title: Try Öcher Reisfladen at Café Van den Daele
new.desc: Aachen's oldest café, founded in 1890 in a crooked old house on the Büchel, serves the local rice pudding tart (Reisfladen) and Printen to a family recipe with Belgian roots.
new.tip: Wander up the creaking stairs to the back rooms with their Aachen-Liège Baroque furniture rather than sitting by the window.
new.q: Café Van den Daele, Büchel 18, Aachen

new.title: Buy a bag of Aachener Printen
new.desc: Printen are Aachen's hard spiced gingerbread, a protected product that may only be baked in and around the city. Nobis, facing the cathedral, is the classic place to stock up, from plain to chocolate coated.
new.tip: Printen get rock hard with time: eat the soft 'Weiche Printen' fresh and buy the crunchy ones to take home.

new.title: Eat Aachener Puttes at the Goldener Schwan
new.desc: Puttes is Aachen's black pudding, often served as Himmel und Ääd with apple sauce and mashed potatoes. The Goldener Schwan serves it in a 15th century house on the Markt.
new.tip: Grab a window seat for a view of the Karlsbrunnen and the town hall.

new.title: Order Sauerbraten with Printen sauce at Zum Wehrhaften Schmied
new.desc: A pub on Jakobstraße since 1914, known for Rhineland Sauerbraten, the marinated pot roast that Aachen thickens with crumbled Printen.
new.tip: In summer ask for a table in the small garden behind the pub.

new.title: Take an ice cream to Burg Frankenberg
new.desc: The Oecher Eis-Treff in the Frankenberger Viertel is a local favourite for homemade ice cream, including a vegan chocolate made with Lindt chocolate from the Aachen factory.
new.tip: Eat it in the Frankenberger Park around the little moated castle, as the locals do.

new.title: Start a Pontstraße evening at Egmont
new.desc: This cult café on Pontstraße, open since 1992, turns from café to bistro to bar through the day, with an Art Deco counter and occasional live music.
new.tip: Order a shawarma plate from Lebanese Akl next door and eat it at Egmont, as students do.

new.title: Grab a beer at the Domkeller on the Hof
new.desc: An old wood-panelled pub behind the cathedral where students, professors and locals spill out onto the Hof on warm nights.
new.tip: Go on a Monday for the live music.

new.title: Have soup and Eifel beer at Café Kittel
new.desc: An Aachen student institution since 1977, loved for its hearty soups and draught beer from the Eifel.
new.tip: It fills up quickly after lectures; come mid-afternoon for a quiet table.

new.title: Drink coffee roasted in the back room at Kaffee Erhard
new.desc: A small coffee shop in the Jakobsviertel where the owner roasts sustainably sourced beans after closing time, so you drink coffee roasted a few metres away.
new.tip: Buy a bag of beans to take home; it is the freshest roast you will find in town.

new.title: Climb the spiral staircase of the Rotes Haus in Monschau
new.desc: A cloth merchant built this house in 1756, and its rococo rooms show how rich Monschau's fine wool trade made the town. The highlight is a free-standing oak staircase over three floors.
new.tip: Visits are by guided tour, which leave regularly; time your Monschau trip around one.

new.title: Look inside the Art Nouveau power station in Heimbach
new.desc: Heimbach's hydroelectric plant from 1905 is still running, with machine halls in Jugendstil style that feel more like a palace than a power plant.
new.tip: The Rurtalbahn train from Düren ends in Heimbach; the station also houses a Nationalpark-Tor with a free exhibition on the Eifel forest.

new.title: Look down on the Rur valley from Burg Nideggen
new.desc: The castle ruin on a red sandstone cliff above the Rur is Nideggen's landmark, with a castle museum inside and long sections of the town wall below.
new.tip: Climbers use the sandstone rocks below the castle; watch them from the path, then visit the Romanesque church of St. Johann Baptist next door.

new.title: Visit the church that coffee built in Schmidt
new.desc: St. Hubertus in Schmidt was destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt with money from post-war coffee smuggling across the Belgian border, so locals call it 'St. Mokka'.
new.tip: Schmidt sits on the ridge above the Rursee: walk down to Eschauel for a swim or a boat afterwards.

new.title: Climb inside the Indemann at Inden
new.desc: A 36 metre steel giant stands on a spoil heap above the Inden open-cast lignite mine, with viewing platforms looking straight into the pit and at the Weisweiler power plant.
new.tip: Come at dusk: tens of thousands of LEDs make the figure glow across the region.

new.title: Walk the bastions of the Zitadelle Jülich
new.desc: Italian architect Alessandro Pasqualini designed this star-shaped Renaissance fortress and the ideal town around it in the 1540s. It is the oldest citadel of its kind north of the Alps.
new.tip: Follow the path along the deep moat, then visit the museum in the palace cellar.

new.title: Climb up to Burg Stolberg
new.desc: Stolberg's castle sits on a limestone rock right in the old town of the former copper capital, where brass and copper makers once worked.
new.tip: The castle courtyards are open during the day; the Torburg museum on weekend afternoons explains the copper, glass and soap trades.

new.title: See the border castle Burg Rode in Herzogenrath
new.desc: This hilltop castle a few hundred metres from Dutch Kerkrade guarded a lucrative toll point for centuries; the Congress of Vienna drew the border right past it.
new.tip: Look for its concert and Platt dialect evenings, or come for the castle festival in June.

new.title: Meet the Döppesbäcker at the pottery museum in Langerwehe
new.desc: Langerwehe has made stoneware for centuries and still has working potteries. The museum in the old parish house tells the story of the 'Wehter Döppesbäcker', from clay mining to the risky kiln firing.
new.tip: Look out for the museum's pottery market, when local potters sell their work.

new.title: Taste mustard ground in the Monschau Senfmühle
new.desc: Since 1882 the Breuer family has ground mustard between old millstones here; they make about 20 varieties of Moutarde de Montjoie.
new.tip: Join a mill tour, then eat in the Schnabuleum next door, where the mustard goes into the cooking.

new.title: Eat a Monschauer Dütchen on the market square
new.desc: Dütchen are Monschau's crisp rolled wafers, filled with cream and fruit. Café Kaulard serves them and other local pastries on the Markt.
new.tip: The terrace looks straight onto the half-timbered square; arrive before midday on weekends.

new.title: Take home Monschauer Venn-Brocken
new.desc: These square chocolates are shaped like the blocks of peat once cut on the High Fens above Monschau, a sweet souvenir sold in the old town.
new.tip: The Schokoladen Café on Stadtstraße is a good place to find them, along with a hot chocolate.

new.title: Eat Flammkuchen in the courtyard of Burg Hengebach
new.desc: Heimbach's castle dates back to around 1000 and now houses an art academy; in its courtyard the Flammkuchenburg bakes thin tarts for hikers and day-trippers.
new.tip: Combine it with the Art Nouveau power station a short walk away along the Rur.

new.title: Hike up to Mariawald for pea soup
new.desc: The former Trappist abbey on the Kermeter above Heimbach is famous for its pea soup, served in the abbey restaurant, with or without sausage.
new.tip: Walk up the 2 km Stations of the Cross path from Heimbach through the national park's beech woods; buy a tin of the soup in the shop for later.

new.title: Visit Monschau's Christmas market
new.desc: On the Advent weekends, stalls fill the narrow lanes from Richters Eck over the Markt to the courtyards behind the Aukirche, between half-timbered houses lit up along the Rur.
new.tip: It gets packed: come on Friday, or take the bus from Aachen to avoid the long parking queues.

new.title: Walk through the wild daffodils of the Perlenbach valley
new.desc: Every spring the meadows of the Perlenbach near Monschau-Höfen turn yellow with wild daffodils, one of the best-known natural spectacles in the Eifel.
new.tip: The easy 5.6 km Kleiner Narzissenrundweg starts at the Höfener Mühle; the Nationalpark-Tor in Höfen has maps and bloom updates.

new.title: Cruise the Rursee from Rurberg
new.desc: The Rursee is one of Germany's largest reservoirs, wrapped in Eifel forest. Excursion boats of the Rursee-Schifffahrt cross the main lake, and quiet electric boats run on the Obersee.
new.tip: Hop off at Eschauel for the bathing beach in summer, or at the Schwammenauel dam to walk back along the shore.

new.title: Spit cherry pits at the Düren Annakirmes
new.desc: One of the biggest funfairs in the Rhineland, with nearly a million visitors over nine days, grew out of a pilgrimage to St. Anne. Opening day brings the cherry pit spitting world championship.
new.tip: Take the train to the Düren Annakirmesplatz stop and stay for the Friday fireworks.

new.title: Make your own sheet of paper at the Papiermuseum Düren
new.desc: Düren grew rich on paper mills along the Rur, and its paper museum lets you scoop pulp from the vat and make your own sheet.
new.tip: Paper-making for walk-in visitors is on Sunday afternoons; the Leopold-Hoesch-Museum for modern art is next door.

new.title: Swim in a former lignite mine at the Blausteinsee
new.desc: Eschweiler's lake filled a lignite pit from 1994 and is now a favourite for swimming, sailing and diving, with a sunken truck and an angel figure for divers.
new.tip: The bathing beach with food is on the western shore; sailing and surfing are on the open water.
